subject: Physics
name: Physics, Units 1 and 2
about: VCE, Heat, nuclear energy, electricity and motion
syllabus: VCE Physics Study Design (from 2023), Units 1 and 2

units.title: Unit 1: How is energy useful to society?

points.title: Waves and their properties
points.brief: Waves have amplitude, wavelength, period and frequency, linked by v = fλ. Light is a transverse wave that needs no medium, unlike sound.

points.title: The electromagnetic spectrum
points.brief: Radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, x-rays and gamma all travel at c in a vacuum. The Sun gives out mostly ultraviolet, visible and infrared.

points.title: Refraction and Snell's law
points.brief: Light bends as it changes speed between materials. Snell's law links the angles to the refractive indices.

points.title: Total internal reflection and optical fibres
points.brief: Beyond the critical angle, light reflects completely inside a material, which lets optical fibres carry signals.

points.title: Dispersion, rainbows and mirages
points.brief: Each colour refracts by a different amount, splitting white light in prisms and raindrops. Mirages come from refraction in warm air.

points.title: Temperature and internal energy
points.brief: Temperature rises as particles gain kinetic and potential energy. Kelvin starts at absolute zero, 273 below Celsius.

points.title: Heat transfer
points.brief: Heat moves by conduction through contact, convection through moving fluids and radiation as electromagnetic waves.

points.title: Specific heat capacity in physics
points.brief: Q = mcΔT gives the energy to change an object's temperature.

points.title: Latent heat
points.brief: Energy absorbed or released during a change of state at constant temperature, Q = mL.

points.title: Cooling by evaporation
points.brief: The fastest particles escape when a liquid evaporates, so the average energy, and the temperature, of what is left falls.

points.title: Black body radiation
points.brief: Hotter objects emit more energy in total, and at a shorter peak wavelength, as Wien's law describes.

points.title: The greenhouse effect and climate
points.brief: Greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit infrared radiation from Earth's surface, warming it. More of them warms it further.

points.title: Nuclear stability
points.brief: The strong nuclear force holds the nucleus together against the repulsion of protons. Unstable nuclei decay.

points.title: Alpha, beta and gamma radiation
points.brief: Alpha particles are helium nuclei, beta-minus are electrons, beta-plus are positrons, and gamma rays are high-energy photons. Each penetrates differently.

points.title: Nuclear equations
points.brief: In a decay, mass numbers and atomic numbers balance on both sides.

points.title: Decay series
points.brief: An unstable isotope decays step by step through other isotopes until it reaches a stable one, shown on a decay series diagram.

points.title: Half-life
points.brief: The time for half the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay.

points.title: Effects of ionising radiation
points.brief: Radiation can damage cells. Absorbed dose is in grays; equivalent and effective dose, in sieverts, allow for the type of radiation and the tissue.

points.title: Medical radioisotopes
points.brief: Radioisotopes are used to find and treat cancers, weighing damage to diseased cells against harm to healthy tissue.

points.title: Nuclear fission
points.brief: A heavy nucleus splits, releasing energy and neutrons. A chain reaction needs enough mass in the right shape, and moderators slow neutrons.

points.title: Nuclear fusion
points.brief: Light nuclei join into a heavier one, releasing energy, as in the Sun.

points.title: Binding energy
points.brief: Fission and fusion release energy because their products are more tightly bound, as the binding energy curve shows. The lost mass becomes energy.

points.title: Nuclear power for Australia
points.brief: Weighing the costs, risks and benefits of nuclear energy as a power source for Australia.

points.title: Charge and current
points.brief: Current is the rate of flow of charge, I = q/t, measured in amperes.

points.title: Potential difference
points.brief: The energy each coulomb of charge gains or loses, measured in volts.

points.title: Models and meters
points.brief: Analogies such as water in pipes help explain current and voltage, each with limits. Ammeters go in series, voltmeters in parallel.

points.title: Resistance and Ohm's law
points.brief: V = IR. Ohmic devices have a constant resistance; others, such as diodes, do not.

points.title: Series circuits
points.brief: Current is the same everywhere, voltages add up to the supply, and resistances add.

points.title: Parallel circuits
points.brief: Voltage is the same across each branch, currents add, and total resistance is less than any one branch.

points.title: Voltage dividers
points.brief: Two resistors in series split the supply voltage in the ratio of their resistances, a basis for sensor circuits.

points.title: Electrical power and energy
points.brief: P = VI, and energy used is power times time, often billed in kilowatt-hours.

points.title: Non-ohmic devices
points.brief: Diodes, thermistors, light dependent resistors and LEDs do not follow Ohm's law, and their I-V graphs show it.

points.title: Circuits in the home
points.brief: Household wiring is mostly parallel, so each appliance gets full voltage and works on its own.

points.title: Safety devices
points.brief: Fuses and circuit breakers stop overloads, earthing protects metal cases, and residual current devices cut power when current leaks.

points.title: Electric shock
points.brief: Current through the body causes harm that grows with size and duration. Knowing the danger levels and first aid saves lives.

units.title: Unit 2: How does physics help us to understand the world?

points.title: Scalars and vectors
points.brief: Scalars have size only, such as speed. Vectors have size and direction, such as velocity.

points.title: Displacement, velocity and acceleration
points.brief: Velocity is the rate of change of displacement and acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.

points.title: Motion graphs
points.brief: Position, velocity and acceleration graphs describe motion, including motion where acceleration changes.

points.title: Equations of motion
points.brief: For constant acceleration, equations such as v = u + at and s = ut + ½at² link the quantities.

points.title: Forces as vectors
points.brief: A force has size and direction and acts at a point. Forces add as vectors, and can be split into components, such as gravity, friction and normal forces.

points.title: Newton's first law
points.brief: An object stays at rest or moves at constant velocity unless a net force acts on it.

points.title: Newton's second law
points.brief: Net force equals mass times acceleration, F = ma.

points.title: Newton's third law
points.brief: When one object pushes on another, the second pushes back with an equal and opposite force.

points.title: Torque and equilibrium
points.brief: Torque is force times perpendicular distance from a pivot. A structure is in equilibrium when forces and torques both balance.

points.title: Momentum and impulse in physics
points.brief: Momentum is mass times velocity. Impulse, force times time, equals the change in momentum, and total momentum is conserved.

points.title: Work and energy
points.brief: Work is force times distance moved. Kinetic energy is ½mv² and gravitational potential energy is mgh.

points.title: Hooke's law
points.brief: An ideal spring stretches in proportion to the force on it, F = -kx, and stores elastic potential energy.

points.title: Conservation of energy and efficiency
points.brief: Energy changes form but is not lost. Power is the rate of transfer, and efficiency is the share that ends up useful.

points.title: Aims, hypotheses, models and theories in physics
points.brief: An aim states what is tested, a hypothesis predicts a result, and models, theories and laws explain or describe patterns.

points.title: Accuracy, precision and validity in physics
points.brief: Accurate results are close to the true value, precise results agree, and valid results measure what was intended.

points.title: Uncertainty and error
points.brief: Random errors scatter results and systematic errors shift them. Uncertainty shows how far a result can be trusted.

points.title: Reporting an investigation
points.brief: A report uses correct terms, units, significant figures and graphs to present findings and link them to physics ideas.
